titles: Radoslav Radev Predicts Strong Enough Planche Trainees With A Perfect Program Can Stay Stuck Forever If Attempt Technique And Muscle Activation Are Bad

Correct Muscle Activation Patterns Matte.text: The most common mistake is assuming that stronger shoulders automatically mean a better planche; in reality, the shoulder is rarely the bottleneck for planche progression—most trainees who fail at the planche do so because of poor lat engagement, core activation, or leg tension, not weak shoulders.

Correct Muscle Activation Patterns Matte.text: Even a world-class athlete cannot compensate for poor technique with strength alone: a world-class calisthenics athlete could not hold the straddle planche with relaxed lats, proving that technique errors are absolute blockers that no amount of strength can bypass.

Correct Muscle Activation Patterns Matte.text: The three most common technique mistakes that stall planche progress are: (1) relaxed core that destroys protraction, (2) relaxed lats that shorten effective arm length, and (3) leaning forward and down instead of forward and up, which drops the body too low. All three are activation/technique errors, not strength deficits.

Correct Muscle Activation Patterns Matte.text: Wrong technique is the primary cause of planche stagnation even when the trainee has a perfect program, adequate training volume, and sufficient strength—trainees who train hard with good programming but wrong muscle engagement can remain stuck on the tuck planche for five months or more, unable to reach the advanced tuck, because the technique error is an absolute blocker that no amount of correct programming can bypass.
